query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Alloying HfMoTaTiZr with a low-density, low-lattice-misfit element such as Sc can reduce the density of the alloy without sacrificing its strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable BCC solid solution with dispersed precipitates
generation.mechanism: Reduced lattice misfit and increased solid solution strengthening
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved yield strength and ductility at room temperature, and maintained yield strength at high temperature, with reduced density
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3 and yield strength of 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at 1000 °C
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to 1000 °C, loading conditions: uniaxial compression
generation.uncertainty: The exact effect of Sc alloying on the microstructure and mechanical properties of HfMoTaTiZr is uncertain and requires experimental verification

falsification_experiment.design: Uniaxial compression tests at room temperature and 1000 °C, microstructural characterization using XRD, SEM, and EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloyed HfMoTaTiZr with Sc exhibits a significant decrease in yield strength or ductility at room temperature, or a significant decrease in yield strength at high temperature, or an increase in density, then the hypothesis is falsified

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Among the various systems of alloying elements studied, the Ta 20 Nb 20 Hf 20 Zr 20 Ti 20 alloy seems to be attractive due to its reduced density of 9.94 g/cm 3 [ [2] , [3] ], few publications [ [4] , [5] , [6] ] deal with thr thermodynamic properties of certain compositions of the Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
